extracted.intended_audience: readers of detective fiction and writers/students studying methods of detection and mystery-plot construction
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for constructing or analyzing detective/mystery narratives and for methodical detective reasoning (how to weigh coincidences, physical evidence, witness testimony, and press reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Calculus of Probabilities to apparent supernatural coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The half-credences...have never the full force of thought—such sentiments are seldom thoroughly stifled unless by reference to the doctrine of chance, or, as it is technically termed, the Calculus of Probabilities.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat startling coincidences skeptically by invoking probability/empirical reasoning rather than supernatural explanation; use mathematical/probabilistic reasoning to explain seemingly marvellous coincidences and to dispel vague half-beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask 'what has occurred that has never occurred before?' (focus on unusual facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the proper question in cases such as this, is not so much ‘what has occurred?’ as ‘what has occurred that has never occurred before?’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for prominences or truly unusual features in the facts of a case; these anomalous elements are more likely to be diagnostic and will guide reason toward the true explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prominences above the ordinary as cues for detection
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘it is by prominences above the plane of the ordinary, that reason feels her way, if at all, in her search for the true’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize and scrutinize striking, atypical details in the scene or testimony—these stand out from routine background and are the most informative leads for solving a mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify the identity of the victim before pursuing other leads
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘it is indispensable that our first step should be the determination of the identity of the corpse with the Marie Rogêt who is missing.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish who the victim actually is (corroborated identification) before tracing motives or suspects; failing to confirm identity can lead investigators (or narrative investigators) to wasted labor or false lines of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that 'ordinary' cases can be harder because many plausible hypotheses exist
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This is an ordinary, although an atrocious instance of crime...because it was not impossible that either of these numerous modes and motives could have been the actual one, they have taken it for granted that one of them must.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facts appear ordinary or familiar, beware: plausibility of many different scenarios increases hypothesis space and makes true solution harder to isolate; exceptional/unusual facts are more decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of newspapers and sensational reporting; they prioritize sensation over truth
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘we should bear in mind that, in general, it is the object of our newspapers rather to create a sensation—to make a point—than to further the cause of truth...The mass of the people regard as profound only him who suggests pungent contradictions of the general idea.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat press accounts as motivated and selective: they may emphasize contradiction or spectacle. Corroborate newspaper claims independently and do not let sensational accounts drive investigative conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on detailed empirical/forensic observation of body and clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive description of the corpse and clothing: rope marks, lace buried in flesh, torn slips wound and knotted, sailor's knot in bonnet strings, excoriations on wrists and back, absence of foam, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and interpret fine-grained physical details (types of knots, placement and character of wounds, condition and pattern of torn clothing) as they can indicate manner of death, staging, transport, and timing; include such specifics in narrative realism and as diagnostic clues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use decomposition and timeline evidence to assess when death occurred
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of L’Etoile’s argument about decomposition: drowned bodies typically require six to ten days to rise; improbable that a body so decomposed could have been in water only two or three days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing timing, employ established empirical norms (decomposition rates, flotation timelines); question and test assumptions about how long a body has been in water or left exposed rather than accepting casual assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require corroboration for eyewitness or single-source identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Skepticism about Beauvais’s identification of the corpse and the press’s reliance on a single witness; the narrative notes the need for stronger proof and the possibility of misrecognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept lone eyewitness identification without cross-checks (family, clothing, distinguishing marks, independent witnesses); seek multiple independent confirmations before fixing identity or public accusation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider staging, misidentification, and alternative explanations explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Press speculation that the corpse might be some other person and that friends/family might be complicit in simulating death; author emphasizes examining the possibility that the body is not the missing person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively entertain and test hypotheses of staging or deliberate misdirection (e.g., planting clothing, substituting bodies) and weigh motives for such fraud; ensure investigative (or plot) steps include elimination or confirmation of these possibilities.
